title: Commercial balloon pilot
sub: Privileges, the heater limit, medical, currency, logging instruction
html:
What the certificate lets you do

  • Fly for hire: act as pilot in command carrying persons or property for compensation or hire (61.133(a)(1)).
  • Teach in balloons with no CFI certificate: give flight and ground training toward a certificate or rating, endorse for the balloon certificate and for solo, and give the training and endorsements for a flight review or recency (61.133(a)(2)(ii); 61.3(d)(3)(i)).
Logging a lesson you give: endorse the student's logbook legibly with a description of the training, the length of the lesson, your signature, your certificate number, and "certificate expiration date or recent experience end date" (61.51(h)(2)). A commercial pilot certificate has no expiration date (61.19(c)). Instructor's practice: name, commercial LTA certificate number, signature, date and notes on the lesson.

The airborne-heater limit (61.133(b))

Checkride inCertificate is limited toLimit removed by
Hot air balloonBalloon with airborne heaterGas balloon experience + instructor endorsement
Gas balloonGas balloonHot air experience + instructor endorsement

Medical (61.23)

Flying for hire
2nd class
Or 1st. Valid to the end of the 12th month after the exam month, at any age
Giving flight training
None
61.23(b)(5)
Private privileges, student, or a balloon checkride
None
61.23(b)(1), (4), (10)

The medical requirement for paid balloon flying took effect May 22, 2023.

Staying current

Flight reviewSince the start of the 24th calendar month before this one: at least 1 h of flight and 1 h of ground training, including Part 91. A passed practical test counts (61.56).
Passengers3 takeoffs and 3 landings in a balloon within the preceding 90 days, as sole manipulator (61.57(a)).
Passengers at nightThe same, to a full stop, between 1 h after sunset and 1 h before sunrise (61.57(b)).

Carry and show

Pilot certificate, photo ID and, when the flight needs one, your medical, on you or readily accessible. Show them on request to the FAA, the NTSB, the TSA or any law enforcement officer (61.3). Report a new permanent mailing address in writing within 30 days (61.60).

To earn it: age 18; at least a private pilot certificate; 35 h as a pilot, including 20 h and 10 flights in balloons, 2 flights as PIC and 10 h of instruction (10+ flights) with two 1-h test-prep flights in the 2 calendar months before the test month, 2 solo flights and a controlled ascent to 3,000 ft above the launch site (61.123(a), (h); 61.129(h)).

title: The balloon itself
sub: Papers aboard, required instruments, inspections, what doesn't apply
html:
Aboard every flight

  • Airworthiness certificate, displayed at the entrance where passengers or crew can read it (91.203(a)(1), (b)).
  • Registration certificate. It expires 7 years after the last day of the month it was issued (91.203(a)(2); 47.40).
  • Operating limitations in the Balloon Flight Manual or on a placard the pilot can see, and you fly within them (31.81(b); 91.9).

Required instruments (31.85)

Every balloon
Altimeter
Rate-of-climb indicator
Hot air adds
Fuel quantity gauge (each fuel cell)
Envelope temperature indicator
Captive gas adds
Compass

Inspections (91.409)

InspectionNeeded whenInterval
AnnualEvery flightWithin the preceding 12 calendar months
100-hour (an annual also satisfies it)Carrying anyone other than crew for hire, or giving flight instruction for hire in a balloon you provideWithin the preceding 100 h time in service. Up to 10 h over only to reach the inspection, and those hours count toward the next 100.

Who answers for what

  • Owner or operator: keeps the balloon airworthy, including airworthiness directives (91.403(a)), and keeps records of the work, its date, and the signature and certificate number of whoever approved return to service; total time; inspection status; and each AD's number, revision date, method of compliance and next due time (91.417).
  • Pilot in command: decides it is in condition for safe flight, and ends the flight if it becomes unairworthy (91.7).
  • Preventive maintenance a pilot may do on a balloon the pilot owns or operates (43.3(g); a sport pilot only on a light-sport category aircraft): small envelope fabric repairs not needing load tape repair or replacement, per the manufacturer; cleaning burner pilot and main nozzles; swapping baskets and burners the type certificate data lists as interchangeable (Part 43 App. A).

Airplane rules that do not apply

91.205 instrumentsPowered aircraft only
91.207 ELTAirplanes only
91.151 fuel reserveAirplanes and rotorcraft only. Plan propane under 91.103 and your flight manual.
91.107 belt briefing and useA free balloon with a basket or gondola is excepted
91.215 and 91.225Only partly: see the radio card

title: Operating rules
sub: Authority, right-of-way, minimum altitudes, alcohol, lights
html:
The pilot in command

  • Final authority for the flight. In an in-flight emergency needing immediate action, deviate from any Part 91 rule as far as needed, and send a written report if the FAA asks (91.3).
  • Before a flight not in the vicinity of an airport, know the weather reports and forecasts, fuel requirements, and alternatives if the flight can't be completed (91.103).
  • No careless or reckless operation that endangers life or property (91.13). Drop nothing that creates a hazard; dropping is allowed with reasonable precautions against injury or damage (91.15).

Right-of-way (91.113)

Aircraft in distressOver all other traffic
BalloonOver any other category of aircraft
Two balloons converging at about the same altitudeThe one on the other's right
OvertakingThe one being overtaken has it

Right-of-way never ends the duty to see and avoid. The pilot giving way may not pass over, under or ahead unless well clear (91.113(b)).

By custom, not regulation: the lower balloon has the right-of-way. The pilot below can't see you through the envelope. Treat it as seriously as a written rule, and before a steep climb confirm with your crew or other pilots that it is clear above you.

Minimum altitudes (91.119)

Except when necessary for takeoff or landing:

Anywhere
High enough for an emergency landing without undue hazard to people or property below
Congested area or open-air crowd
1,000 ft
above the highest obstacle within 2,000 ft horizontally
Elsewhere
500 ft
above the surface. Over open water or sparsely populated areas: no closer than 500 ft to any person, vessel, vehicle or structure.

No balloon exception: 91.119(d) covers only helicopters, powered parachutes and weight-shift-control aircraft.

Also

  • Alcohol and drugs (91.17): no acting as a crewmember within 8 h of a drink, while under the influence, at 0.04 alcohol concentration or more, or on a drug that impairs. Except in an emergency, carry no one who appears intoxicated.
  • Near other aircraft (91.111): never close enough to create a collision hazard. Formation flight only by arrangement with each pilot, and never with passengers for hire.
  • Lights (91.209): lighted position lights from sunset to sunrise.

title: NTSB Part 830
sub: What counts as an accident, what to report at once, and deadlines
html:
Is it an accident? (830.2)

An occurrence between the time anyone boards with the intention of flight and the time everyone has gotten off, in which anyone suffers death or serious injury, or the aircraft receives substantial damage.

Serious injury
  • Hospital for more than 48 h, starting within 7 days of the injury
  • Any broken bone, except simple fractures of fingers, toes or nose
  • Severe bleeding, or nerve, muscle or tendon damage
  • Any internal organ involved
  • Second- or third-degree burns, or burns over more than 5% of the body
Substantial damage

Damage or failure that harms structural strength, performance or flight characteristics and would normally need major repair or replacement of the part.

Not substantial: small punctured holes in the skin or fabric, among other listed minor damage.

Notify the NTSB immediately (830.5)

After any accident, and after any of these listed incidents even if no one is hurt:

  • Flight control system malfunction or failure
  • A required flight crewmember unable to perform normal duties because of injury or illness
  • In-flight fire
  • Aircraft collision in flight
  • Damage to property other than the aircraft estimated over $25,000 (repair, or fair market value if a total loss, whichever is less)
  • An overdue aircraft believed to have been in an accident

The rest of the 830.5 list covers turbine engines, propellers, rotors, large multiengine aircraft, cockpit displays, collision-avoidance alerts and air carriers.

NTSB Response Operations Center: 844-373-9922 or 202-314-6290

What to tell them (830.6)

Aircraft type, nationality and registration · owner and operator · pilot in command · date and time · last departure point and intended landing · position from an easily defined point · number aboard, killed and seriously injured · nature of the accident, weather and damage, so far as known · any explosives, radioactive or other dangerous articles aboard.

After the call

Wreckage (830.10)Don't move it until the NTSB takes custody, except to free injured or trapped people, protect it from further damage, or protect the public. If you must move it, sketch, note and photograph where it lay. Keep all records.
Written report (830.15)NTSB Form 6120.1/2 within 10 days of an accident, or after 7 days if an overdue aircraft is still missing. For a listed incident, only if the NTSB asks. Each crewmember able to do so attaches a statement.

title: Density altitude and lift
sub: Pressure altitude, standard temperature, density altitude, worksheet
html:
Three steps

1 · Pressure altitude
PA = elevation + (29.92 − altimeter) × 1,000
2 · Standard temperature
ISA = 15 °C − 2 °C per 1,000 ft of PA
3 · Density altitude
DA ≈ PA + 120 × (OAT − ISA)

Worked example

Field elevation 1,400 ft, altimeter 29.82, OAT 30 °C.

Pressure altitude1,400 + (29.92 − 29.82) × 1,000 = 1,400 + 100 = 1,500 ft
Standard temperature15 − 2 × 1.5 = 12 °C
Density altitude1,500 + 120 × (30 − 12) = 1,500 + 2,160 = 3,660 ft
3,660 ft
The balloon performs as if the field were 2,260 ft higher.

What it does to lift

  • Buoyancy equals the weight of the air the envelope displaces. Heating the air inside makes it less dense, so the balloon rises when it weighs less than the air it pushes aside.
  • High elevation, low pressure, high temperature and high humidity all mean thinner air and less lift at the same envelope temperature: more heat for the same load, more fuel, less margin under the envelope's limit.
  • Rough rule: 1,000 cubic feet of heated air lifts about 20 lb.
  • Burner performance drops about 4% per 1,000 ft.
  • Maximum gross weight is in your flight manual; its performance chart reads lift from ambient temperature, envelope temperature and pressure altitude.

Worksheet

StepFlight 1Flight 2
Field elevation (ft)
Altimeter setting (inHg)
(29.92 − altimeter) × 1,000
Pressure altitude
ISA = 15 − 2 × (PA ÷ 1,000)
OAT (°C)
(OAT − ISA) × 120
Density altitude

The 120 ft per °C step is a common rule of thumb, an approximation. For PA 10,000 ft at 20 °C it gives 13,000 ft; the Aviation Weather Handbook's computed answer is 12,700 ft. A flight computer or the app's chart is closer.
sources: FAA-H-8083-25C Ch. 4 (standard atmosphere, pressure and density altitude)

title: Preflight, crew and passengers
sub: Go/no-go, launch site, crew briefing, passenger briefing, pre-launch
html:
Before you go (91.103; PTS Area III)

  • Weather reports and forecasts, PIREPs, SIGMETs and G-AIRMETs; hazards to balloon flight; a go/no-go decision.
  • Fuel requirements, and alternatives if the flight can't be completed.
  • A course plotted from winds aloft; airspace, obstructions and terrain; landing areas; NOTAMs.
  • Operating weight, maximum load, fuel quantity and endurance; envelope temperatures, including never-exceed and maximum continuous.

Launch site (PTS V.A)

Size and surface · access and obstacles · surface wind and winds aloft · obstacles nearby · landing areas downwind · a suitable time for the conditions.

Crew briefing (PTS V.B)

  • Designate a crew chief if appropriate, and give each crewmember their duties.
  • Brief layout and assembly, tie-off, inflation, in flight, landing, recovery and emergency procedures.
  • Agree on a common means of communication: hand signals and/or two-way radio.
  • Tell them the expected direction of flight and time aloft. Check that all equipment is on board.

Layout, inspection, inflation (PTS V.C–E)

Fuel system secure, leak-free, correct pressure · cables and lines attached per the flight manual · inspect basket, envelope, suspension and handling lines, vent or deflation system, burner, fuel system, instruments · tie off as the manufacturer specifies · vent/deflation lines positioned and secured.

Passenger briefing (BFH Ch. 6, 8)

Give it before inflation and again once you decide to land:

  1. Stand where shown: usually the rear of the basket; the front in a high-wind landing.
  2. Face the direction of travel (or away from it, if that is what you briefed).
  3. Feet and knees together, knees bent. Avoid the word "brace": legs stay springy.
  4. Hold on tight, in two places.
  5. Stay in the basket until the pilot says to get out.
No seat-belt briefing is required in a basket balloon (91.107(a)). Except in an emergency, carry no one who appears intoxicated (91.17(b)).

Pre-launch check (PTS V.F–G)

Loose items secured · wind, temperatures and obstructions reviewed · final instrument check · vent/deflation lines secured · final coordination with crew, including signals and emergency procedures · bring the balloon to equilibrium · no conflict with traffic, above and around.

title: Emergencies and propane
sub: First moves for balloon emergencies; propane facts and refueling
html:
Fly the balloon first. Resolve the situation, then check the flight manual or checklist. In an emergency you may deviate from Part 91 as far as needed (91.3(b)). Your flight manual's procedure governs.

First moves (BFH Ch. 7–8)

Vent or deflation line lostOnly the burner controls descent. Stay low, land in the largest area you can, expect rebound and drag in wind; a poorer field may be worth it to avoid power lines.
Pilot light outTwo burners: fly on the other; try a relight using both. One burner: igniter or striker; else crack the blast valve slightly and light the stream, or use the backup system. Land as soon as practical.
Fuel leak or fire at a fittingShut off the fuel source. A small fire at a fitting: shut off, then snuff it with a gloved hand.
ThermalKeep the envelope at least at its equilibrium temperature; don't vent to descend. It usually releases you higher.
High-wind landingLowest safe altitude to a large field, deflation line clear. Committed: brief passengers, fuel valves off, drain lines, pilot lights off. At 15 mph you cover 220 ft in the 10 s a burn takes to work.
Water landingPassengers clear of the basket in case it inverts; hold on to it, it floats. A deflated envelope sinks; tanks float.
Power linesWatch for them on every approach. If contact can't be avoided, follow your flight manual.

The checkride also asks about blast valve failure, fuel exhaustion and your emergency and survival gear (PTS Area X): answer from your flight manual.

Propane (BFH Ch. 2, App. A)

  • Boils at −44 °F (butane 32 °F), but in the tank it is at the outside air temperature.
  • Vapor is heavier than air and pools low; the odorant is ethyl mercaptan.
  • Escaped liquid makes about 6,800 times its volume of combustible mixture.
  • The fixed maximum liquid level gauge marks 80% full; the relief valve normally opens near 375 psi.
°Fpsi

Cold mornings: add nitrogen through a regulator if the flight manual allows; vapor-feed pilot systems may not tolerate it. Cancelled, with a rise of more than 30° coming? Bleed the pressure through the fixed liquid level gauge.

Refueling: open air, never from inside the basket or a closed trailer or van · no smoking · strikers disabled · chase vehicle off · gloves. When the spit valve spits: main tank valve, then spit valve, then supply line, then bleed the lines.
sources: FAA-H-8083-11B Ch. 8 (thermals, high-wind and water landings, refueling)

title: Checkride day
sub: Prerequisites, what to bring, the 11 areas and what they ask
html:
Before you can test (61.39)

Knowledge test passed within the 24 calendar months before the test month · age 18 and the experience · instructor endorsement: trained within the 2 calendar months before the month of application, ready, and weak knowledge-test areas reviewed · signed application.

Bring (PTS checklist)

For the balloon: airworthiness and registration certificates · operating limitations · maintenance records showing inspections and AD compliance · balloon flight manual.
Equipment: the PTS, a current chart, computer and plotter, flight log, current AIM.
For you: photo and signature ID · pilot certificate · medical certificate or statement (the PTS lists it; 61.23(b)(10) needs none for a balloon checkride) · FAA Form 8710-1 with your instructor's signature · knowledge test report · logbook with endorsements · Form 8060-5 if retesting · approved school graduation certificate, if any · examiner's fee.

Areas of operation (FAA-S-8081-18A)

AreaWhat they ask
I Fundamentals of instructingLearning and teaching; instructor responsibilities (always) plus at least one other task
II Technical subjectsAeromedical factors, scanning, principles of flight and false lift, Parts 1, 61, 91 and 830, airspace, the logbook entries and endorsements you will give
III Preflight preparationCertificates, medical and inspections; weather and go/no-go; a planned maximum-duration flight with real-time weather; performance; systems
IV Preflight lessonTeach one maneuver from Areas VII–XI as you would to a learner
V Preflight proceduresLaunch site, crew briefing, layout, inspection, inflation, basket management, pre-launch check
VI Airport operationsFrequencies, phraseology, ATC clearances
VII Launches and landingsNormal and over-obstacle launches; normal and steep approaches; normal and high-wind landings. Over-obstacle launch and high-wind landing go oral if conditions don't allow.
VIII Performance maneuversAscents, level flight, descents, rapid ascent and descent, contour flying, obstacle avoidance, tethering, winter and mountain flying
IX NavigationAirspace, landmarks against the chart, position, fuel, flight duration
X Emergency operationsMalfunctions, emergency and survival gear, water landing, thermals
XI PostflightRecovery with the landowner, deflation and pack-up, refueling and propane
sources: FAA-S-8081-18A Section 1, Areas of Operation I–XI
